metadata.source: Fremont Gurdwara Sahib – Waheguru Ji Ka Khalsa, Waheguru Ji Ki Fateh

entries.question: What should I wear when entering the Darbar Sahib?
entries.answer: Please dress modestly and cover your head with a rumala (head scarf) before entering the Darbar Sahib. Avoid sleeveless tops, short skirts, or any clothing considered immodest. Head coverings are available at the entrance for those who need them.

entries.question: Do I need to remove my shoes before entering?
entries.answer: Yes, all footwear must be removed before entering the Gurdwara. There are shoe racks outside the main entrance. This is a sign of humility and respect for the sacred space (pavan dargah).

entries.question: How do I greet the Sangat when I arrive?
entries.answer: Upon entering, you greet fellow sangat with 'Waheguru Ji Ka Khalsa, Waheguru Ji Ki Fateh' (often shortened to 'Fateh'). This is the traditional Sikh greeting that acknowledges the Khalsa and victory belonging to Waheguru.

entries.question: What do I do when I approach the Guru Granth Sahib Ji?
entries.answer: Approach the Guru Granth Sahib Ji with reverence. Bow (matha tek) by kneeling and touching your forehead to the floor as a sign of respect and submission. You may offer a contribution to the golak (offering box) if you wish, but it is not required.

entries.question: Where should I sit in the Darbar Sahib?
entries.answer: Sit on the floor in the sangat, facing the Guru Granth Sahib Ji. Men and women typically sit on separate sides (left and right), though this may vary by Gurdwara. Never sit with your feet pointing toward the Guru Granth Sahib Ji or turn your back to it.

entries.question: Can I take photos or videos inside the Darbar Sahib?
entries.answer: Photography and videography inside the Darbar Sahib are generally not permitted during religious services (diwan). If you wish to capture a memory, please ask the Gurdwara staff for permission. Always be respectful and avoid disrupting the sangat.

entries.question: What is Matha Tek and how is it done correctly?
entries.answer: Matha Tek is the act of bowing before the Guru Granth Sahib Ji. Kneel with both knees, place both hands on the floor, then bow your forehead to touch the ground. Rise slowly and join the sangat. It is done as an act of gratitude and devotion (seva of the mind).

entries.question: What is Karah Prashad and how do I receive it?
entries.answer: Karah Prashad is a sacred sweet pudding made of flour, butter (ghee), and sugar. It is distributed to all sangat after the Ardas (prayer). Receive it with both hands cupped together. Everyone receives Karah Prashad equally, symbolizing the equality of all people.

entries.question: What is the Ardas and when does it happen?
entries.answer: Ardas is the Sikh communal prayer offered to Waheguru. It is performed at the beginning and end of religious ceremonies, after completion of any significant reading (path), and before Karah Prashad is distributed. Stand respectfully with hands folded (together) during Ardas.

entries.question: Can non-Sikhs visit and participate in the Darbar Sahib?
entries.answer: Absolutely! The Gurdwara is open to people of all faiths, backgrounds, and walks of life. The Sikh principle of sarbat da bhala (welfare of all) means everyone is welcome. Simply follow the basic etiquette: cover your head, remove shoes, and be respectful.

entries.question: What happens during the Diwan (congregation)?
entries.answer: The Diwan includes Kirtan (devotional singing of Gurbani), Katha (religious discourse), Simran (meditation on Waheguru's name), and concludes with Ardas and distribution of Karah Prashad. It is a beautiful spiritual gathering of the sangat.

entries.question: Is it okay to talk or use my phone during the Kirtan?
entries.answer: Please silence your phone before entering the Darbar Sahib. Avoid talking during Kirtan and Katha as it disrupts the sangat's focus and is disrespectful to the Guru Granth Sahib Ji. If you need to speak, step outside quietly.

entries.question: What is Langar and who can eat there?
entries.answer: Langar is the community kitchen and free meal served in every Gurdwara. It is open to all people, regardless of faith, background, gender, or economic status. Langar embodies the Sikh value of equality and seva (selfless service). Everyone eats together, symbolizing unity.

entries.question: Is the Langar food vegetarian?
entries.answer: Yes, Langar is always strictly vegetarian (and typically free of eggs as well). This ensures that the meal can be shared by all people regardless of dietary restrictions or religious beliefs. No meat, fish, or eggs are served in the Langar hall.

entries.question: When is Langar served at Fremont Gurdwara Sahib?
entries.answer: Langar is served every day after the morning and evening Diwans. On weekends and special occasions (Gurpurab), Langar is served throughout the day. Please check the Gurdwara's schedule for specific timings as they may vary.

entries.question: Do I need to cover my head in the Langar hall?
entries.answer: Yes, head covering is required in the Langar hall as a sign of respect, just as in the Darbar Sahib. Head scarves are available at the entrance if you do not have one.

entries.question: How do I serve or participate in Langar seva?
entries.answer: Langar seva (volunteering in the community kitchen) is open to all. You can help with preparing food, serving the sangat, washing dishes, or cleaning. Simply approach the Gurdwara management or the Langar kitchen and express your wish to do seva. It is a deeply fulfilling spiritual practice.

entries.question: Where do I sit during Langar?
entries.answer: In the Langar hall, everyone sits on the floor in rows (pangat), side by side. This practice reinforces equality — no one sits higher than another. After eating, please return your thali (plate) and utensils to the cleaning area to assist the seva team.

entries.question: Can I donate food or supplies for Langar?
entries.answer: Yes! Donations of vegetarian food items, spices, flour, vegetables, cooking oil, and other supplies are warmly welcomed. You can also donate money to the Gurdwara to support the Langar. Contact the Gurdwara office for specific needs and drop-off information.

entries.question: Is there a fee to eat Langar?
entries.answer: No, Langar is completely free of charge for everyone. It has been a Sikh tradition since Guru Nanak Dev Ji established it in the 15th century. The meal is funded entirely by donations (daswandh) and volunteer seva from the sangat.

entries.question: What foods are typically served in Langar?
entries.answer: Typical Langar includes dal (lentil soup), sabzi (vegetable curry), roti (flatbread) or rice, and sometimes kheer or other desserts. On special occasions like Gurpurab, a more elaborate meal may be prepared. All food is made with love and devotion (seva).

entries.question: Where is Fremont Gurdwara Sahib located?
entries.answer: Fremont Gurdwara Sahib serves the Bay Area Sikh community in Fremont, California. For the exact address, directions, and parking information, please visit the Gurdwara's official website or contact the Gurdwara office directly.

entries.question: What are the Gurdwara's visiting hours?
entries.answer: The Gurdwara is generally open daily for morning and evening services. On weekends and Gurpurabs (Sikh celebrations), it may be open for extended hours. Please check the Gurdwara's website or contact them directly for the most current schedule.

entries.question: What is Waheguru?
entries.answer: Waheguru is the Sikh name for the formless, timeless Creator — often translated as 'Wondrous Enlightener.' It is the primary name used in Sikhi to refer to God. Repeating 'Waheguru' is a form of Simran (meditation) and is central to Sikh spiritual practice.

entries.question: What is the Guru Granth Sahib Ji?
entries.answer: The Guru Granth Sahib Ji is the eternal, living Guru of the Sikhs — the holy scripture that contains the sacred hymns (Gurbani) of the Sikh Gurus and other saints. It is treated with the utmost reverence, like a living Guru. All Sikh ceremonies center around it.

entries.question: What is a Gurpurab?
entries.answer: A Gurpurab is a Sikh holy day commemorating significant events in Sikh history — most commonly the birth or martyrdom anniversaries of the ten Sikh Gurus. Special extended Diwans, Akhand Path (continuous scripture reading), and festive Langar are held during Gurpurabs.

entries.question: Can I bring children to the Gurdwara?
entries.answer: Yes, children are very welcome at the Gurdwara! It is a wonderful opportunity to introduce them to Sikh values and culture. Please guide children to follow the etiquette — covering their heads and removing shoes — and ensure they behave respectfully during the Diwan.

entries.question: What is Seva and why is it important in Sikhi?
entries.answer: Seva means selfless service — serving others without expectation of reward. It is one of the three pillars of Sikhi (along with Nam Japna — meditation, and Vand Chhakna — sharing). Doing seva at the Gurdwara, whether in Langar or the Darbar, is considered a profound spiritual practice.

entries.question: What should I avoid doing in the Darbar Sahib?
entries.answer: Avoid pointing your feet toward the Guru Granth Sahib Ji, turning your back to it, loud talking or laughing, using phones, or eating inside the Darbar. Never enter under the influence of alcohol or tobacco. These practices are part of Gurdwara Maryada (code of conduct).

entries.question: What is Gurdwara Maryada?
entries.answer: Gurdwara Maryada refers to the code of conduct and etiquette observed within the Gurdwara. It is guided by the Sikh Rehat Maryada — the official code of the Sikh way of life approved by the Akal Takht. Maryada ensures that the Gurdwara remains a sacred and respectful space for all sangat.
